tldr: Researchers have developed SBLR, a method that achieves zero-shot transfer of policies trained on a point-cloud and force "oracle sensor" to real-world tactile sensors—without building any physics simulation of the tactile sensor itself. By using bottlenecked latent reconstruction to deliberately simulate the drop in information content, the approach achieves high success rates of 85–97.5% on real-world peg insertion and gear meshing tasks using GelSight Mini and DIGIT sensors.
hero_caption: An overview of the proposed SBLR framework. Instead of elaborately modeling specific tactile sensors in simulation, the policy is trained on an oracle representation composed of point clouds and contact forces. SBLR bridges the information gap with real sensors via bottlenecked latent reconstruction in the latent space, enabling zero-shot transfer to diverse real-world sensors such as GelSight Mini and DIGIT.
overview:
Tactile sensors are a powerful asset when robots perform contact-rich tasks like parts assembly or gear meshing. However, faithfully reproducing tactile sensors in simulation is remarkably difficult. Mechanical structure, internal optics, and elastomer deformation characteristics vary widely across different sensors, requiring substantial domain expertise and validation effort to build physical models.

To overcome this, the authors took a counterintuitive approach: what if we simply stop trying to simulate real tactile sensors altogether? They define ideal information that is readily available inside the simulator—specifically, object and fingertip point clouds along with contact force vectors (Point Force Composition, or PFC)—as an "oracle sensor." Reinforcement learning is first conducted purely using this oracle information. Then, using random contact data collected in both simulation and the real world, generative models (Rectified Flow) are trained to bidirectionally transform between the real sensor latent features and the oracle latent features.

A key challenge here is the "information disparity." Because the oracle sensor holds richer information than the real tactile sensor, perfectly reconstructing the oracle from the real sensor is impossible. To handle this, the authors introduce a two-stage RL scheme featuring "bottlenecked latent reconstruction": the oracle features are first compressed into estimated real sensor features and then reconstructed back into oracle features. This trains the policy in advance to cope with the information loss inherent to real sensors.

In experiments on challenging tasks such as Peg Insertion and Gear Meshing, using two visually and mechanically distinct vision-based tactile sensors (GelSight Mini and DIGIT), SBLR achieved 85–97.5% success rates—outperforming a physics-based simulation baseline (TacSL) by 7.5–15%. It provides a remarkably practical framework that frees researchers from the tedious chore of building sensor-specific simulations.
contributions: Proposed SBLR, a framework that trains policies on an oracle sensor composed of point clouds and forces and transfers them to the real world without building any physical model of a specific tactile sensor.
Designed a two-stage reinforcement learning architecture that reconstructs latent features via bidirectional Rectified Flow to adapt to the information disparity between the oracle and real sensors.

Developed an unsupervised method to construct pseudo-pairs from autonomous play data—collected by randomly probing fixed objects in both simulation and the real world—using nearest-neighbor search over proprioceptive state transitions.
Achieved 85–97.5% zero-shot success rates on real-world Peg Insertion and Gear Meshing tasks with both GelSight Mini and DIGIT, outperforming a physics-based tactile simulator baseline.

sections.heading: Why simulate tactile sensors when you don't have to?
sections.summary: Tactile feedback is vital for contact-rich tasks, but faithfully reproducing diverse tactile sensors in simulation is extremely challenging. This paper introduces SBLR, a novel method that learns on a simulator-native oracle sensor and transfers to real hardware via latent space alignment and bottlenecked latent reconstruction.
sections.details:
For robots to manipulate objects dexterously, large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation followed by zero-shot transfer to real hardware is considered a promising direction. However, the biggest bottleneck remains tactile sensor simulation. Tactile sensors involve complex physical phenomena such as elastomer deformation and internal camera optics, and their designs differ drastically across models. Rebuilding physical models every time a new sensor arrives is impractical, and attempting to bridge the gap with domain randomization often wipes out subtle contact signals altogether.

To address this, the authors propose Sim2Real via Bottlenecked Latent Reconstruction (SBLR). As a paradigm shift, instead of mimicking real sensors, the method leverages an "oracle sensor" that is trivially accessible in simulation. Specifically, it defines Point Force Composition (PFC)—consisting of complete point cloud data of the fingertips and object along with contact force vectors—as the oracle, and trains an initial policy on it.

Naturally, there is an information gap between the oracle and real sensors, with the oracle possessing significantly richer information. It is fundamentally impossible to achieve perfect reconstruction of oracle latents from real sensor latents. Therefore, this approach builds a "bottlenecked reconstruction" loop using Rectified Flow (RF) to project oracle features down to real sensor features and back to oracle features. A lightweight second-stage RL fine-tuning on this reconstructed space adapts the policy to become resilient against sensor-specific information loss.

captions.F1: Conceptual overview of SBLR. Instead of constructing physics-based sensor simulations, the policy is trained via RL on point clouds and forces (PFC). Bottlenecked latent reconstruction learned from unpaired random contact data in simulation and the real world then adapts the policy to information loss when deploying real sensors.

sections.heading: How does SBLR advance unified tactile representations, physics simulation, and domain alignment?
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes itself within three lines of research: unified tactile representations, physics-based tactile simulation, and cross-domain representation alignment. SBLR sets itself apart by eliminating the need for sensor simulation entirely while bridging the information disparity.
sections.details:
To clarify its positioning, the work is compared against three research areas:

- Unified Tactile Representation
Recent work focuses on extracting common representations across different tactile sensors or integrating them into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, these focus on extracting shared information across sensors, still requiring sensor-specific simulations when performing reinforcement learning. In contrast, the oracle sensor in SBLR is explicitly designed to contain strictly richer information than real sensors, avoiding the burden of sensor simulation.

- Physics-based Tactile Simulation
Simulators like Taxim and TacSL have greatly improved the fidelity of vision-based tactile simulation through GPU parallelization and advanced optical rendering. However, they require FEM parameters and optical calibration for each sensor, demanding considerable domain expertise. SBLR takes the approach of avoiding sensor-specific simulation altogether.

- Cross-Domain Representation Alignment
Studies also exist that align latent representations between simulation and reality, or between humans and robots (such as TactSpace and TactAlign). However, they rely on FEM models, are restricted to camera images, or are confined to imitation learning settings; none have demonstrated zero-shot RL transfer without sensor simulation.

sections.heading: The setup: How to tackle real hardware without sensor simulation
sections.summary: The goal is to train a policy in simulation and achieve high success rates on real hardware without using physical simulations of real tactile sensors. Simulator-native oracle information (PFC) is available in simulation, and unpaired random contact data bridges the gap to the real world.
sections.details:
The problem addressed in this work is to deploy a policy $\pi_\theta$ trained solely in simulation onto real hardware in a zero-shot manner, without running any physics simulation of the target tactile sensor.

On the simulation side, instead of a sensor simulation, the policy uses an oracle observation $\mathbf{p}$ termed Point Force Composition (PFC). PFC consists of complete point clouds of the robot fingertips $\mathbf{X}_i$ and target object $\mathbf{X}_o$, along with contact force vectors $\mathbf{f}_i$ acting on the fingertips ($\mathbf{p} := (\{\mathbf{X}_i, \mathbf{f}_i\}_i, \mathbf{X}_o)$). These are extracted directly from the internal physics engine state with zero added computational overhead.

In the real environment, however, the robot only receives raw tactile sensor readings such as images $\mathbf{c}$. To bridge this gap, "random-play data" is collected in both simulation and the real world by letting the robot repeatedly make random contacts against fixed objects. Since real-world data collection is costly, only a modest amount is collected, while large quantities are generated in simulation. The ultimate objective is to obtain a policy that achieves high task success during real deployment when the oracle $\mathbf{p}$ is unavailable and only $\mathbf{c}$ is observed.

sections.heading: Inside SBLR: Four steps and bottlenecked latent reconstruction
sections.summary: The methodology consists of four steps: (1) unpaired random-play data collection and nearest-neighbor pseudo-pairing, (2) self-supervised encoder pre-training and bidirectional Rectified Flow training, (3) stage-1 RL with the oracle, and (4) stage-2 RL adaptation via bottlenecked latent reconstruction.
sections.details:
The overall workflow of SBLR comprises the following steps:

- IV-A Alignment Data Construction
Replicating identical contacts between the real world and simulation to form exact pairs is infeasible. Instead, objects are fixed at known positions while the robot executes random contact probing motions. When the object pose is shared, similar transitions in robot proprioception $(\mathbf{q}_{t-1}, \mathbf{q}_t)$ indicate similar contact states. Nearest-neighbor search over these transitions is used to form pseudo-pairs.

- IV-B Pre-training Feature Encoders
Because raw point clouds and high-resolution images are high-dimensional, they are mapped into low-dimensional latent spaces. Simulated point clouds are encoded using Point-MAE and contact forces with a dedicated autoencoder, which are combined into a PFC latent representation $\mathbf{z}_p$. Real tactile images are encoded using an MAE into latent representation $\mathbf{z}_c$.

- IV-C Bidirectional Transformation Networks via Rectified Flow
Because the relationship between the oracle and the real sensor exhibits one-to-many information asymmetry, Rectified Flow is adopted rather than deterministic mappings to model multi-modal distributions. Two networks are trained on the pseudo-pairs: $f_{p \rightarrow c}$ to generate real sensor features from oracle features, and $f_{c \rightarrow p}$ to reconstruct oracle features from real sensor features.

- IV-D Stage-1 RL Training with PFC
A base policy $\pi_\theta$ is first trained via RL taking the PFC latent representation $\mathbf{z}_p$ as input. At this stage, no specific real sensor is considered. To prevent overfitting to pristine PFC values, small Gaussian noise is added during training: standard deviations of 0.5 mm in position, 0.29° in rotation for object poses, and 0.3 N for contact forces.

- IV-E Stage-2 Adaptation via Bottlenecked Latent Reconstruction
This is the core contribution of the paper. Oracle features $\mathbf{z}_p$ are mapped via $f_{p \rightarrow c}$ to estimated real sensor features $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_c$, and then mapped back to the oracle space via $f_{c \rightarrow p}$ to produce reconstructed features $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_p$. Because the real sensor lacks the full information of the oracle, passing through this round-trip inherently introduces information loss and distortion. Performing lightweight stage-2 RL fine-tuning with $\hat{\mathbf{z}}_p$ trains the policy to adapt robustly to this real-sensor-specific information drop.

- IV-F Real-World Inference
During real-world deployment, the observed tactile image $\mathbf{c}$ is encoded into $\mathbf{z}_c$, mapped into the oracle space via $f_{c \rightarrow p}$, and passed to the adapted policy to output control actions.

sections.heading: Results: Outperforming physics-based simulation on hardware
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted via ablation experiments in simulation and assembly tasks on real robots equipped with GelSight Mini and DIGIT sensors. On hardware, SBLR attained 85–97.5% success rates, outperforming the physics-based tactile simulation baseline (TacSL) by 7.5–15%.
sections.details:
Experiments evaluated the framework through both simulation and hardware benchmarks.

- V-A & V-B Simulation Experiments (Factory Tasks)
Using Isaac Lab, three tasks were evaluated: Peg Insertion, Gear Meshing, and Nut Threading. TacSL was used as a synthetic "pseudo-real" environment to isolate and assess the sensor modality gap. SBLR was compared against Discrete Contact Position (DCP, binning contacts into 8 discrete categories), Optimal Transport (OT), No Tactile, and an ablation without stage-2 adaptation (PFC + RF). SBLR consistently outperformed the ablation, showing substantial gains especially on Nut Threading, which requires high geometric precision. Furthermore, it closely approached the performance of an upper-bound Image Oracle trained directly on ground-truth tactile images.

- V-C Real-World Experiments (Hardware Validation)
Hardware tests were conducted on Peg Insertion and Gear Meshing using two distinct sensors: the high-resolution, compliant GelSight Mini, and the lower-resolution, stiffer elastomer DIGIT. Alignment data consisted of just 256 autonomous probing episodes (40 minutes) on fixed objects without human intervention.
Over 40 evaluation trials per condition, SBLR achieved 97.5% on peg insertion and 92.5% on gear meshing with GelSight Mini. With DIGIT, it achieved 87.5% on peg insertion and 85.0% on gear meshing. Compared to a strong physics-based baseline (TacSL trained with domain randomization), SBLR outperformed it by 7.5–15% across all settings. While physics simulators are vulnerable to unmodeled factors like elastomer flatness assumptions and 3D-printed fixture tolerances, SBLR learns latent transformations directly from real contact data, preventing divergence from the physical environment.

sections.heading: Discussion and limitations: What works and what remains open
sections.summary: While sensor modality gaps are effectively eliminated, dynamics gaps such as friction and control latency remain, and random contact probing may not cover intricate contact states for highly complex tasks. Extensions to larger foundation models (VLAs) are also highlighted.
sections.details:
While the framework shows compelling practical utility, the authors frankly discuss its limitations and future directions:

- Remaining Dynamics Gap
SBLR resolves the modality gap between tactile sensor readings and oracle representations, but it does not magically eliminate dynamics gaps such as friction coefficients, joint control stiffness, or communication delays between simulation and the real world. In this work, standard domain randomization was still used alongside SBLR to handle dynamics variations.

- Coverage of Alignment Data
Autonomous random probing against fixed objects is fully hands-free, but it may not adequately cover extremely fine and constrained contact regimes, such as aligning nut thread grooves. For such precision tasks, incorporating human teleoperation data to enrich the contact distribution represents a promising avenue for improvement.

- Future Outlook and Generality
The lightweight stage-2 adaptation design of SBLR is well-suited for integration with large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. Rather than retraining a massive model from scratch, rapidly running only stage-2 bottleneck adaptation whenever a new tactile sensor is introduced could evolve this method into an agile platform across diverse robot hardware.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A new standard for tactile Sim2Real
sections.summary: SBLR completely bypasses tactile sensor simulation, achieving real-world transfer via point-cloud and force oracle representations combined with bottlenecked latent reconstruction. Its effectiveness has been demonstrated across diverse sensors and contact tasks.
sections.details:
This paper presented SBLR, a framework for tactile Sim2Real transfer that avoids modeling specific tactile sensors altogether. By training policies on a simulator-native oracle sensor (PFC) and adapting them to real sensor information loss via bottlenecked latent reconstruction with bidirectional Rectified Flow, policies transfer seamlessly without paired data.

Through Factory benchmarks in simulation and real-world assembly tasks on GelSight Mini and DIGIT sensors, SBLR demonstrated superior robustness and success rates compared to conventional physics-based simulation methods. By eliminating the weeks of engineering typically spent on sensor modeling and parameter tuning, this work marks a significant milestone toward accelerating contact-rich robotic manipulation research.

sections.heading: Appendix: How pseudo-pairs are extracted from unpaired contact data
sections.summary: The appendix details the algorithm for extracting high-quality contact pseudo-pairs from autonomously collected random probing data using nearest-neighbor search over proprioceptive state transitions.
sections.details:
Because intentionally replicating identical contact states across simulation and real hardware is virtually impossible, accurately extracting pseudo-pairs from unpaired data is central to SBLR.

- A-A Data Collection Procedure
The target object (peg or gear) is mounted at a known fixed position. The robot end-effector pose is randomly sampled around the object, the gripper closes to initiate contact, and small translation and rotation probing motions are performed. Because the object is secured, automatic resets and continuous data collection proceed without human intervention.

- A-B Proprioceptive Transition Nearest-Neighbor Pairing
Since object positions are identical, similar robot end-effector/joint states $\mathbf{q}_t$ imply similar contact states. Normal forces appear in proprioception as slight depressions due to elastomer compliance, but shear forces cannot be discerned from a single static step. Thus, state transitions from the previous step $S_t = (\mathbf{q}_{t-1}, \mathbf{q}_t)$ are defined, and similarity is measured using the distance metric $D(S_t^s, S_t^r) = \|\mathbf{q}_t^s - \mathbf{q}_t^r\|_2 + \lambda \|\mathbf{q}_{t-1}^s - \mathbf{q}_{t-1}^r\|_2$ with $\lambda < 1$. Control actions themselves are excluded from similarity metrics because dynamics discrepancies (like friction) produce different physical responses under identical commands. The top $k$ simulation candidates below a threshold $\delta$ are selected as nearest-neighbor pseudo-pairs.

takeaways: Instead of struggling to build detailed physical tactile simulators, utilizing simulator-native point clouds and contact forces (PFC) as an "oracle sensor" is remarkably effective.

Because information loss is inevitable when moving from an oracle to real sensors, passing latents through an oracle -> real -> oracle "bottleneck reconstruction" during RL instills robustness against missing information.

Combining automated random probing on fixed objects with nearest-neighbor search over proprioceptive transitions enables high-quality contact pseudo-pair collection without human labels or supervision.
The approach achieved high success rates not just on the compliant GelSight Mini but also on the stiffer, lower-resolution DIGIT sensor, proving its adaptability across varied sensor designs.
limitations: While the framework bridges the tactile sensor modality gap, system dynamics gaps (friction, stiffness, delays) still require separate mitigation, such as domain randomization.
Relying on random probing around fixed objects may fail to sufficiently cover narrow, specialized contact distributions required for ultra-precise tasks like thread engagement.
Each task and target object currently requires approximately 40 minutes of real-world probing data collection and individual Rectified Flow training, falling short of fully task-agnostic alignment.
